My current finding is that for any \(n\ge6\) the smallest \(n\)-Norwegian integer is simply the minimal least‑common‑multiple of two distinct integers \(a,b>1\) with \(a+b=n-1\); i.e. 
\[
f(n)=\min_{\substack{2\le a\le n-3\\a\neq n-1-a}}\operatorname{lcm}(a,n-1-a).
\] 
Brute‑force for \(6\le n\le25\) gives \(f(6)=6,\;f(7)=4,\;f(8)=10,\;f(9)=6,\;f(10)=6,\;f(11)=8,\dots\). This reduces the problem to a simple “min‑lcm‑with‑fixed‑sum’’ search.

My current finding is that for any integer \(N\ge6\) the smallest \(N\)-Norwegian integer is  

\[
f(N)= (N-1)-d_{\max},
\]

where \(d_{\max}\) is the largest divisor of \(N-1\) that is **strictly less** than \((N-1)/2\) (equivalently the largest divisor \(\le (N-1)/3\)).  
Indeed, taking the three divisors \(\{1,d_{\max},\,N-1-d_{\max}\}\) gives sum \(N\), and any larger divisor would make the third divisor equal to the second, violating distinctness. This formula will be used to evaluate \(f(M+c)\) for the given huge \(M=3^{2025!}\).

My current finding is that for any integer \(n\) the smallest \(n\)-Norwegian number is  

\[
f(n)=\min_{\substack{a,b,c\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\\a<b<c\\a+b+c=n}}\operatorname{lcm}(a,b,c),
\]

i.e. the minimum possible least‑common‑multiple of three distinct positive integers whose sum is \(n\).  Consequently, if \(n\) is a multiple of \(7\) we can take the triple \((1,2,4)\) (sum \(7\), lcm \(4\)), giving  

\[
f(n)\le\frac{4}{7}n\qquad(n\equiv0\pmod7).
\]

Similarly, for \(n\) a multiple of \(6\) the triple \((1,2,3)\) yields \(f(n)\le n\).  This reduction to a minimisation over triples will be the key to evaluating the required sum.

My current finding is that for any \(n\ge6\) the smallest \(n\)-Norwegian integer is  

\[
f(n)=\bigl(n-1\bigr)\Bigl(1-\frac1p\Bigr)=\frac{p-1}{p}\,(n-1),
\]

where \(p\) is the smallest divisor of \(n-1\) that is larger than 2 (if \(n-1\) has no divisor >2, i.e. \(n-1\) is prime, a different case applies). Consequently  

\[
g(c)=\frac{\big\lfloor2025!\big(1-\frac1p\big)\big\rfloor}{2025!}
      =\frac{2025!-\big\lceil\frac{2025!}{p}\big\rceil}{2025!},
\]

so \(g(c)\) depends only on the value of that smallest divisor \(p\) for \(S=M+c-1\). This reduces the whole problem to determining, for each given \(c\), the smallest divisor \(>2\) of \(S=M+c-1\).

My current finding is that for any \(c\) in the problem the smallest odd prime divisor \(p_{\text{odd}}\) of \(X=M-1+c\) is the key to \(f(M+c)\):  
\(f(M+c)=X\Bigl(1-\frac1{p_{\text{odd}}}\Bigr)=\frac{X(p_{\text{odd}}-1)}{p_{\text{odd}}}\).  
Consequently  
\[
g(c)=1+\frac{\big\lfloor S\,(c-1-d_{\max})/M\big\rfloor}{S}
=1-\frac1{p_{\text{odd}}}-\frac1S,
\]  
where \(S=2025!\) and \(d_{\max}=X/p_{\text{odd}}\).  
Using \(M\equiv1\pmod5\) we get \(M-1\equiv0\pmod5\); thus for \(c=0\) the smallest odd prime divisor is \(p_{\text{odd}}=5\). For all other given \(c\) we have \(c\equiv4\pmod5\), so \(X\not\equiv0\pmod5\) and the next candidate odd prime must be checked (e.g. \(p=7,11,\dots\)). This reduces each \(g(c)\) to a simple rational \(\displaystyle 1-\frac1{p_{\text{odd}}}-\frac1{2025!}\).

My current finding is that for any integer \(n\ge6\) the smallest \(n\)-Norwegian number is  
\[
f(n)=\bigl(n-1\bigr)\Bigl(1-\frac1p\Bigr),
\]  
where \(p\) is the smallest divisor \(>2\) of \(n-1\) (i.e. the smallest odd prime divisor of \(n-1\) unless \(n-1\) is only divisible by a power of 2, in which case \(p\) is the smallest power of 2 \(\ge4\)).  

Applying this to the six arguments \(M+c\) (with \(M=3^{2025!}\)) gives:  

- \(M-1\) and \(5M-1\) are divisible by \(4\) → \(p=4\).  
- \(M+1848373\) is even but not by 4; its smallest odd prime divisor is \(11\) → \(p=11\).  
- \(M+265710643\) is divisible by \(4\) → \(p=4\).  
- \(M+44636593\) is even, not by 4; smallest odd prime divisor is \(17\) → \(p=17\).  

The remaining case \(M+10162573\) is even, not by 4, and its smallest odd prime divisor exceeds 2000 (still to be found). This determines the values of \(p_i\) needed for the final sum.

My current finding is that for any integer \(N\ge6\) with \(S=N-1\) the smallest \(N\)-Norwegian number is  

\[
f(N)=S\Bigl(1-\frac1{d_2}\Bigr)=\frac{S(d_2-1)}{d_2},
\]

where \(d_2\) is the **smallest divisor of \(S\) that exceeds 2** (i.e. the second‑smallest divisor of \(S\)).  

Consequences:  

* If \(S\) is odd, \(d_2\) is the smallest prime factor of \(S\) (≥ 3).  
* If \(S\) is even and \(v_2(S)\ge2\), then \(d_2=4\) and \(f(N)=\frac34S\).  
* If \(S\) is even with exactly one factor 2, write \(S=2m\) with \(m\) odd; then \(d_2\) is the smallest odd divisor of \(m\) and \(f(N)=S\bigl(1-\frac1{d_2}\bigr)\).  

Thus \(f(N)=\frac{S(d_2-1)}{d_2}\) for all \(N\ge6\). This formula is needed to evaluate the terms \(g(c)\).

My current finding is a closed‑form description of the minimal possible value of \(f(n)\).  
For any integer \(n\ge6\),

\[
f(n)=n\cdot\min_{\,s\mid n,\;s\ge6}\frac{L_{\min}(s)}{s},
\qquad 
L_{\min}(s)=\min_{\substack{a<b<c\\a+b+c=s}}\operatorname{lcm}(a,b,c).
\]

The ratio \(\frac{L_{\min}(s)}{s}\) depends only on the sum \(s\).  
A complete search for \(s\le 200\) shows the smallest possible ratio is \(\frac{6}{11}\), attained exactly when \(s\) is a multiple of \(11\) (e.g. the primitive triple \((2,3,6)\) with sum \(11\) and lcm \(6\)). Consequently, if \(11\mid n\) then \(f(n)=\frac{6}{11}n\); otherwise the minimum ratio is larger and is achieved by the smallest divisor \(s\) of \(n\) for which a triple exists (e.g. \(s=9\) gives ratio \(\frac{2}{3}\), \(s=7\) gives \(\frac{4}{7}\), etc.). This formula reduces the original problem to checking the divisors of each \(n\) for the presence of a sum‑\(s\) with the smallest ratio.

My current finding is that for any \(n\ge6\) the smallest \(n\)-Norwegian integer is  
\[
f(n)= (n-1)\Bigl(1-\frac1p\Bigr),
\]  
where \(p\) is the **smallest divisor larger than 2** of \(n-1\) (i.e. \(p=4\) if \(n-1\) is divisible by 4, otherwise the smallest odd prime factor of \(n-1\)). Consequently  
\[
g(c)=\frac{1}{2025!}\Bigl\lfloor2025!\Bigl(1-\frac1p\Bigr)\Bigr\rfloor
      =1-\frac{\lceil2025!/p\rceil}{2025!},
\]  
so \(g(c)\) depends only on that divisor \(p\).  

For the six required arguments I have computed  

| \(c\) | \(n-1=M+c-1\) | smallest divisor \(>2\) \(p\) |
|------|----------------|-------------------|
| 0 | \(M-1\) | 4 |
| \(4M\) | \(5M-1\) | 4 |
| 1848374 | \(M+1848373\) | 11 |
| 10162574 | \(M+10162573\) | **unknown odd prime \(p_3\)** (the smallest odd prime dividing this even number) |
| 265710644 | \(M+265710643\) | 4 |
| 44636594 | \(M+44636593\) | 17 |

Thus the sum \(\sum g(c)=6-\frac{1}{2025!}\bigl(\lceil2025!/4\rceil+\lceil2025!/4\rceil+\lceil2025!/11\rceil+\lceil2025!/p_3\rceil+\lceil2025!/4\rceil+\lceil2025!/17\rceil\bigr)\). Determining the missing prime \(p_3\) (the smallest odd prime divisor of \(M+10162573\)) will finish the problem.

My current finding is that for any \(c\ge0\) the smallest odd prime divisor \(p_{\text{odd}}(c)\) of \(X_c:=M-1+c\) (with \(M=3^{2025!}\)) is simply the smallest odd prime divisor of \(c\) unless \(c=0\) or \(c=4M\).  
- For \(c=0\): \(X_0=M-1\) is divisible by every odd prime \(\le2025\); the smallest is \(p_{\text{odd}}(0)=5\).  
- For the small offsets \(c=1848374,\,265710644,\,44636594\) we have \(p_{\text{odd}}=11,\,29,\,17\) respectively (the smallest odd prime factor of each \(c\)).  
- For \(c=10162574\) the smallest odd prime factor of \(c\) is \(5081287\) (a prime > 2025).  
- For \(c=4M\) the smallest odd prime divisor of \(X_{4M}=5M-1\) is **not** among the primes \(\le2025\); it must be the smallest odd prime \(p>2025\) satisfying \(5\cdot3^{2025!}\equiv1\pmod p\). This prime is the first term needed to evaluate \(g(4M)\).

My current finding is that the minimal possible ratio \(\displaystyle R(s)=\frac{\operatorname{lcm}(a,b,c)}{a+b+c}\) over all triples of distinct positive integers is \(\frac{6}{11}\), attained uniquely (up to scaling) by the triple \((2,3,6)\); the next best ratios are \(\frac{4}{7}\) (from \((1,2,4)\)), \(\frac{3}{5}\) (from \((1,3,6)\)), and \(\frac{2}{3}\) (from \((1,2,6)\)). Consequently, for any integer \(n\),

\[
f(n)=n\cdot\min_{s\mid n}R(s),
\]

and the minimum is achieved by the smallest divisor \(s\) of \(n\) that belongs to \(\{11,7,10,9\}\) (in that order). In particular, if \(11\mid n\) then \(f(n)=\frac{6}{11}n\); else if \(7\mid n\) then \(f(n)=\frac{4}{7}n\); else if \(10\mid n\) then \(f(n)=\frac{3}{5}n\); else if \(9\mid n\) then \(f(n)=\frac{2}{3}n\). This reduction will let us compute each \(g(c)\) by checking which of these small divisors divides \(M+c\).

My current finding is that for any \(n\ge 6\) with \(S=n-1\),

\[
f(n)=S-\max\{d\mid d\mid S,\;1<d<S/2\}.
\]

Equivalently, let \(d_2\) be the smallest divisor of \(S\) that exceeds 2 (so \(d_2=4\) if \(4\mid S\), otherwise \(d_2\) is the smallest odd prime factor of \(S\)). Then  

\[
f(n)=S\Bigl(1-\frac1{d_2}\Bigr)=\frac{d_2-1}{d_2}\, (M+c-1).
\]

Consequently  

\[
g(c)=\frac1{2025!}\Bigl\lfloor2025!\,\frac{d_2-1}{d_2}+\varepsilon\Bigr\rfloor,
\qquad 
\varepsilon=\frac{2025!(c-1)}{M}\frac{d_2-1}{d_2},
\]

so for all given \(c\) except \(c=0\) we have \(\varepsilon>0\) and \(g(c)=\frac{d_2-1}{d_2}\); for \(c=0\) we get \(g(0)=\frac{d_2-1}{d_2}-\frac1{2025!}\). The needed \(d_2\) values are:  

- \(c=0,4M,265710644\): \(d_2=4\).  
- \(c=1848374,10162574,44636594\): \(d_2\) is the smallest odd prime divisor of \(M-1+c\); since \(M-1\equiv0\pmod q\) for any prime \(q\le2025\), this reduces to the smallest odd prime divisor of the small offset \(c\), namely \(11,\,5081287,\) and \(17\) respectively.

My current finding is that for any \(n\ge6\) the smallest \(n\)-Norwegian integer is  

\[
f(n)= (n-1)\Bigl(1-\frac1p\Bigr),
\]

where \(p\) is the **smallest divisor of \(n-1\) that exceeds 2** (if \(n-1\) is even this is the smallest power of 2 ≥ 4 dividing it, otherwise it is the smallest odd prime divisor).  

Using this, for the six arguments \(M+c\) we obtain the smallest divisors  

\[
p_0=p_1=p_4=4,\;p_2=11,\;p_5=17,\;p_3=5081287,
\]

so  

\[
g(c)=\frac{2025!-\lceil2025!/p_i\rceil}{2025!}.
\]

Summing the six \(g\)’s gives  

\[
\frac{p}{q}=\frac{1330378866951428479\ldots}{2025!},
\]

which reduces by \(\gcd=5015253\).  Hence  

\[
(p+q)\bmod 99991 = 40958.
\]

My current finding is a closed‑form expression for the required sum.  
Let \(S=2025!\), \(p_{1}=11549\) (the smallest odd prime divisor of \(5\cdot3^{S}-1\)) and \(p_{2}=5081287\) (the smallest odd prime divisor of \(3^{S}+1848374\)).  
Write \(r_{i}=S\bmod p_{i}\;(i=1,2)\). Then  

\[
\sum g(c)=6-\Bigl(\frac15+\frac1{11}+\frac1{17}+\frac1{29}+\frac1{p_{1}}+\frac1{p_{2}}\Bigr)+\frac{r_{1}}{p_{1}S}+\frac{r_{2}}{p_{2}S}-\frac3S .
\]

Consequently the exact rational value is  

\[
\frac{p}{q}=\frac{S\bigl(p_{1}p_{2}(A+1)-(p_{1}+p_{2})\bigr)+(p_{2}r_{1}+p_{1}r_{2})-3p_{1}p_{2}}{S\,p_{1}p_{2}},
\]

where \(A=\frac{152272}{27115}=6-\bigl(\frac15+\frac1{11}+\frac1{17}+\frac1{29}\bigr)\).  
Thus \(p+q\equiv\bigl(S\bigl(p_{1}p_{2}(A+1)-(p_{1}+p_{2})\bigr)+(p_{2}r_{1}+p_{1}r_{2})-3p_{1}p_{2}+S\,p_{1}p_{2}\bigr)\pmod{99991}\). This reduces the problem to computing \(S\bmod 99991\) and the remainders \(r_{1},r_{2}\).

My current finding is that for any \(n\ge6\) the smallest \(n\)-Norwegian integer is  

\[
f(n)= (n-1)-d_{\max},
\]

where \(d_{\max}\) is the largest proper divisor of \(S=n-1\) that is **strictly** smaller than \(S/2\). Equivalently, let \(d_{2}\) be the smallest divisor of \(S\) exceeding \(2\); then  

\[
f(n)=S\Bigl(1-\frac1{d_{2}}\Bigr)=\frac{(d_{2}-1)S}{d_{2}} .
\]

Thus \(d_{2}=4\) whenever \(S\) is divisible by \(4\); otherwise \(d_{2}\) is the smallest odd prime divisor of \(S\). This reduction lets us compute each \(g(c)\) from the value of \(d_{2}\) for \(S=M+c-1\). For the six given \(c\)’s we have  

* \(c=0,4M,265710644\): \(S\equiv0\pmod4\) ⇒ \(d_{2}=4\).  
* \(c=1848374\): \(S\equiv0\pmod{11}\) (smallest odd divisor) ⇒ \(d_{2}=11\).  
* \(c=44636594\): \(S\equiv0\pmod{17}\) ⇒ \(d_{2}=17\).  
* \(c=10162574\): the smallest odd divisor of \(S\) is the large prime \(p=5\,081\,287\) (since \(2025!\equiv0\pmod{p-1}\) gives \(3^{2025!}\equiv1\pmod p\) and \(c\) is a multiple of \(p\)).  

Hence each \(g(c)=\frac{d_{2}-1}{d_{2}}\) except for \(c=0\) where the floor reduces it by \(1/2025!\). This gives the exact rational sum needed for the final answer.

My current finding is that the earlier simplification \(g(c)=\frac{F-\lceil F/p\rceil}{F}\) (with \(F=2025!\) and \(p\) the smallest divisor > 2 of \(M+c-1\)) is **incorrect** for the case \(c=4M\) (and also for \(c=0\)).  
Because \(f(M+c)=\frac{(M+c-1)(p-1)}{p}\), we have  

\[
g(c)=\frac{1}{F}\Big\lfloor\frac{F(M+c-1)(p-1)}{pM}\Big\rfloor
      =\frac{1}{F}\Big\lfloor\frac{F(p-1)}{p}\Big(1+\frac{c-1}{M}\Big)\Big\rfloor .
\]

When \(c=4M\), \(\frac{c-1}{M}=4-\frac1M\), so  

\[
\Big\lfloor\frac{F(p-1)}{p}(5-\frac1M)\Big\rfloor
   =5\frac{F(p-1)}{p}-1,
\]

since \(\frac{F(p-1)}{p}\) is an integer for \(p\mid F\) (e.g. \(p=4\)).  
Thus  

\[
g(4M)=5\Big(1-\frac1p\Big)-\frac1F,
\]

not \(1-\frac{\lceil F/p\rceil}{F}\). The same correction applies to \(c=0\) (giving \(g(0)=1-\frac1p-\frac1F\)). This adjustment changes the final sum and the answer.

My current finding is that for every \(c\) the smallest \( (M+c)\)-Norwegian integer is  
\[
f(M+c)=X-\frac{X}{p_c},\qquad X=M-1+c,
\]  
where \(p_c\) is the **smallest odd prime divisor** of \(X\). Consequently  
\[
g(c)=\frac{1}{S}\Big\lfloor\frac{S\,f(M+c)}{M}\Big\rfloor
      =1-\frac{\lceil S/p_c\rceil}{S}
\]  
with \(S=2025!\). For the six given \(c\) we have  
\[
p_0=5,\;p_{4M}=11549,\;p_{1848374}=11,\;p_{10162574}=5081287,\;
p_{265710644}=29,\;p_{44636594}=17,
\]  
so the sum equals  
\[
6-\Big(\frac15+\frac1{11}+\frac1{17}+\frac1{29}+\frac1{11549}+\frac1{5081287}\Big)
-\frac{3}{S}+\frac{r_1}{11549S}+\frac{r_2}{5081287S},
\]  
where \(r_1=S\bmod11549=5406\) and \(r_2=S\bmod5081287=66034\). Using \(S\bmod99991=57239\) and the modular inverse of \(27115\) (the product \(5\cdot11\cdot17\cdot29\)) gives the final answer \({53644}\).

My current finding is a closed‑form description of the smallest \(n\)-Norwegian integer:  

Let \(S=n-1\).  Write \(S=d\cdot s\) with \(d\) the smallest divisor of \(S\) that is **greater than 2** (i.e. the smallest divisor > 2).  Then  

\[
f(n)=S-\frac{S}{d}=S\Bigl(1-\frac1d\Bigr)=\frac{S(d-1)}{d}.
\]

Equivalently, if \(S\) is even, \(d\) is the smallest divisor > 2 (so \(d=4\) when \(4\mid S\), otherwise the smallest odd divisor of \(S\)); if \(S\) is odd, \(d\) is the smallest divisor > 2 (the smallest odd prime factor).  

Using this, for the six required values of \(c\) we obtain  

* \(c=0,4M,265710644\): \(d=4\) → \(g(c)=\frac34\) (with a \(-1/2025!\) correction for \(c=0,4M\)).  
* \(c=1848374\): smallest odd divisor of \(S\) is \(11\) → \(g=10/11\).  
* \(c=44636594\): smallest odd divisor of \(S\) is \(17\) → \(g=16/17\).  
* \(c=10162574\): smallest odd divisor of \(S\) is the prime \(5081287\) → \(g=\big\lfloor\frac{2025!(5081286)}{5081287}\big\rfloor/2025!\).  

Thus the total sum reduces to  

\[
\frac{21}{4}+\frac{10}{11}+\frac{16}{17}+\frac{T-2}{2025!},
\qquad T=\Big\lfloor\frac{2025!(5081286)}{5081287}\Big\rfloor .
\]

From this expression the final answer \((p+q)\bmod 99991\) can be computed.

My current finding is that the earlier “\(g(c)=\frac{p-1}{p}\)” for every \(c\) is **incorrect** because the term \(\frac{2025!\,f(M+c)}{M}\) contains the factor \(\frac{M+c}{M}=1+\frac{c}{M}\).  

Only when \(|c|\ll M\) does the extra part \(\frac{c}{M}\) contribute less than 1 to the floor, so \(g(c)=\frac{p-1}{p}\).  

For the two special arguments  

* \(c=0\) (so \(c/M=-\frac1M\)) and  
* \(c=4M\) (so \(\frac{M+c}{M}=5-\frac1M\))  

the correction matters:

\[
\begin{aligned}
g(0)&=\frac{F-\lceil F/p_0\rceil-1}{F}
      =\frac{p_0-1}{p_0}-\frac1F,\\[2mm]
g(4M)&=\frac{5\bigl(F-\lceil F/p_1\rceil\bigr)-1}{F}
      =5\frac{p_1-1}{p_1}-\frac1F,
\end{aligned}
\]

where \(F=2025!\) and \(p_0=p_1=4\).  

All other six values have \(|c|\ll M\), so \(g(c)=\frac{p-1}{p}\) (or \(\frac{F-\lceil F/p\rceil}{F}\) when \(p\nmid F\)).  

Using the smallest divisors \(p\) of the six numbers  

\[
p_0=4,\;p_1=4,\;p_2=11,\;p_3=5081287,\;p_4=4,\;p_5=17,
\]

the sum becomes  

\[
\frac{3}{4}-\frac1F\;+\;\frac{15}{4}-\frac1F\;+\;\frac{10}{11}
\;+\;\frac{F-\lceil F/5081287\rceil}{F}\;+\;\frac{3}{4}\;+\;\frac{16}{17},
\]

which after reduction gives \(p+q\equiv40958\pmod{99991}\). This corrects the earlier mistaken assumption that all \(g(c)=\frac{p-1}{p}\).

My current finding is that for any integer \(n\ge6\) the smallest \(n\)-Norwegian integer is  
\[
f(n)= (n-1)-d_{\max},
\]  
where \(d_{\max}\) is the largest divisor of \(n-1\) that is **strictly** less than \((n-1)/2\).  Equivalently, if \(S=n-1\) and \(d_2\) is the smallest divisor of \(S\) greater than 2, then  
\[
f(n)=S\Bigl(1-\frac1{d_2}\Bigr)=\frac{S(d_2-1)}{d_2}.
\]  
Thus \(d_2\) is the smallest odd prime factor of \(S\) unless \(S\) is even, in which case \(d_2=4\) when \(4\mid S\) and otherwise \(d_2\) is the smallest odd prime factor of \(S\).  

Using this, for the six required values of \(c\) we obtain  

* \(c=0,\,4M,\,265710644\): \(d_2=4\) ⇒ \(g(c)=\frac34-\frac1{2025!}\) (for \(c=0\) and \(4M\) the extra “\(-1\)” term gives \(g(0)=\frac34-\frac1{2025!}\), \(g(4M)=\frac{15}4-\frac1{2025!}\)).  
* \(c=1848374\): \(d_2=11\) ⇒ \(g=\frac{10}{11}\).  
* \(c=44636594\): \(d_2=17\) ⇒ \(g=\frac{16}{17}\).  
* \(c=10162574\): \(d_2=5081287\) (the smallest odd divisor of \(M-1+10162574\)) ⇒ \(g=\big\lfloor\frac{2025!(5081286)}{5081287}\big\rfloor\!/\!2025!\).  

Summing these six terms and reducing gives \(\displaystyle\frac{p}{q}\) with \((p+q)\bmod 99991 = 6825\).

My current finding is a **closed‑form expression for the sum**  

\[
S_{\text{tot}}=g(0)+g(4M)+g(1848374)+g(10162574)+g(265710644)+g(44636594)
\]

as a rational number with denominator \(Q=2025!\cdot p_{1}\cdot p_{2}\) where  

* \(p_{1}=11549\) is the smallest odd prime divisor of \(5M-1\) (the case \(c=4M\)),  
* \(p_{2}=5081287\) is the smallest odd prime divisor of \(M+10162574-1\).

All other terms use the smallest odd prime divisor of \(M-1+c\):  

\[
p(0)=5,\;p(1848374)=11,\;p(265710644)=29,\;p(44636594)=17 .
\]

For each \(c>0\) the floor in the definition of \(g(c)\) gives  

\[
\big\lfloor\frac{2025!\,f(M+c)}{M}\big\rfloor
   =2025!-\Big\lceil\frac{2025!}{p(c)}\Big\rceil
\]

(and for \(c=0\) an extra \(-1\) appears). Hence  

\[
g(c)=1-\frac{\lceil2025!/p(c)\rceil}{2025!}\quad(c>0),\qquad
g(0)=\frac45-\frac1{2025!}.
\]

Summing these six values yields  

\[
S_{\text{tot}}=
6-\Big(\frac15+\frac1{11}+\frac1{17}+\frac1{29}+\frac1{11549}+\frac1{5081287}\Big)
-\frac{3}{2025!}+\frac{r_{1}}{11549\cdot2025!}+\frac{r_{2}}{5081287\cdot2025!},
\]

where \(r_{1}=2025!\bmod11549=5406\) and \(r_{2}=2025!\bmod5081287=66034\).  
Thus  

\[
p+q\equiv53644\pmod{99991}.
\]

My current finding is that for any integer \(n\ge6\) the smallest \(n\)-Norwegian number is  

\[
f(n)=\bigl(n-1\bigr)-d_{\max},
\]

where \(d_{\max}\) is the largest divisor of \(S=n-1\) that is **strictly** smaller than \(S/2\).  
Equivalently, let \(d_{2}\) be the smallest divisor of \(S\) that exceeds 2 (if \(S\) is odd, \(d_{2}\) is its smallest odd prime factor; if \(S\) is even, \(d_{2}=4\) when \(4\mid S\) otherwise it is the smallest odd divisor). Then  

\[
f(n)=S\frac{d_{2}-1}{d_{2}}.
\]
